rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1375, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir, salok 199
rows.original: ਕਬੀਰ ਜੀਅ ਜੁ ਮਾਰਹਿ ਜੋਰੁ ਕਰਿ ਕਹਤੇ ਹਹਿ ਜੁ ਹਲਾਲੁ (Gurmukhi given from the researcher's memory; the search results showed only the English)
rows.translation: Sant Singh Khalsa (as on sikhsamridhi.com and SikhiWiki)
rows.says: Those who use force to kill living beings (jīa) and call it lawful (halāl) will have to answer for it when God calls for their account.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider rule (rule 7). Jīa means any living being, so it reaches every person K1 protects, whatever their faith, sex, age or status. It also denies that calling a killing lawful or religious makes it right. Its immediate target is ritual slaughter, and Sikhs disagree on whether such verses forbid eating meat. That dispute is about animals (exclusion (e)) and does not narrow the verse's reach for people. It states no self-defence exception, so it asks more than K1, which still counts (METHOD.md section 3, wider rules). It is not about courts or war.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): sikhsamridhi.com, a Gurbani database giving Gurmukhi, transliteration and translation, and two SikhiWiki pages place salok 199 on ang 1375 with this sense ('they oppress living beings and kill them, and call it proper'), followed by salok 200 on force as tyranny. rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1103, Rāg Mārū, Bhagat Kabir

rows.says: You kill living beings and call it a righteous act. Then tell me, brother, what would you call unrighteous? Killing is treated as the plainest case of wrongdoing, and a religious label cannot change that.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider rule (rule 7) that reaches everyone. It rejects religious justification for killing, which bears directly on K1's protection of unbelievers, heretics and 'the wicked'. Kabir is addressing those who kill in ritual (the surrounding lines were not checked in this search). Whether it also forbids killing animals is disputed in the tradition (exclusion (e)), but people are within jīa whichever reading is taken. Not about courts or war.

rows.bearing: K0, and support for K1: a wider rule against using force on anyone (rule 7). Killing someone for gain, or in anger, is force at its extreme, so it falls inside the rule. support.reconciliation:
Counted texts. The Guru Granth Sahib (Tier 1, accepted by every Sikh group) is the only counted text. No passage found in it permits, commands or approves a private killing of anyone: not daughters, wives, servants, people of other faiths, or 'the wicked'. Its teaching runs the other way. Kabir's saloks condemn killing living beings by force and calling it lawful (ang 1375) or righteous (ang 1103). Farid forbids breaking any heart, because the One dwells in all (ang 1384). He also teaches against anger and revenge (ang 1382, 1378). Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal person frightens no one (ang 1427). Because these texts state no exception, they ask more than K1. The finding that nothing in the scripture permits private killing rests on targeted searches, not a full reading, and the counter-evidence hunt is another researcher's.

How the tradition reconciles non-violence with the use of the sword. From the sixth Guru onwards, the tradition accepted armed force as a last resort against tyranny and in defence of the weak. Its standard statement is Zafarnama couplet 22: when every other means has failed, it is lawful to take the sword. This text is in the Dasam Granth, which corpus.md flags as contested, so it is context only. Sikh writers (SikhiWiki; Naujawani, reporting a British Library discussion; both secondary) read it as a 'last resort' rule. The tradition reconciles the two strands by limiting deadly force to defence and to war against tyranny. That is the shape of K1's exception plus exclusion (b). It does not reconcile them by permitting killing for gain, anger or revenge, which Farid and Kabir rule out (K0). Guru Nanak's Babarvani (ang 360, verified only on a secondary site) adds the war-time line: fighting between the strong is not complained of, but slaughter of the defenceless is a wrong that someone must answer for.

The meat dispute. Kabir's verses on killing living beings are read in two ways. The SGPC's Sikh Rehat Maryada forbids only ritually slaughtered (kutha) meat, which implies a narrower, anti-ritual reading. Other Sikhs (for example the Namdharis; general knowledge, not verified here) read them as forbidding all killing for food. This narrowing concerns animals (exclusion (e)). Neither reading takes people outside the verses.

Household killing. The Sikh Rehat Maryada makes explicit that a Sikh must not kill a daughter or keep company with a daughter-killer (Article XVI). It is Tier 2, the official code of the SGPC and Akal Takht for mainstream Khalsa Sikhs (approved 1945, published 1950); its standing is that of a modern body's authority, and it decides nothing on its own. The Akal Takht's 2001 directive extends this to female foeticide (outside the corpus; before birth, context only). No Guru Granth Sahib verse on infanticide was found, so for newborns K1 rests on the wider rules, which reach all living beings.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule, rule 7); not contradicted in any counted text found
K1.reason: Kabir's saloks at ang 1375 (salok 199, VERIFIED (search) on sikhsamridhi.com and SikhiWiki) and ang 1103 (VERIFIED (search) on SearchGurbani) condemn killing living beings, even when it is called lawful or righteous. Jīa reaches every person of any faith, sex, age or status, newborns included (rule 9). Farid's 'break no heart, for the One dwells in all' (ang 1384) and Guru Tegh Bahadur's 'frighten no one' (ang 1427) support them. All are Tier 1 and accepted by every Sikh group. The texts state no self-defence exception, so they ask more than K1, which still counts. Caveats: the strongest direct texts target ritual killing and are rated Clear teaching rather than Explicit. The ang 1375 row is confirmed on a Gurbani database not on the project's named list. No counted text was found that permits private killing of any class. The Rehat Maryada's explicit ban on killing daughters is Tier 2 and is reported beside the label (rule 1). Zafarnama 22 (contested Dasam Granth) limits deadly force to a last resort and falls under K1's exception and exclusion (b). The result depends on the separate counter-evidence search finding nothing that changes it.

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: Everything that teaches K1 also teaches K0, the narrower wording (ang 1375, 1103, 1384). In addition, the scripture addresses K0's motives directly. Farid salok 78 (ang 1382, VERIFIED (search)) says to answer evil with good and not let anger take hold. Farid salok 7 (ang 1378, VERIFIED (search)) says not to strike back at those who strike you. Kabir saloks 187 and 200 (ang 1374 to 1375, VERIFIED (search)) say that force used on others is tyranny, even when called lawful. Ang 199 (no bullying of the weak) supports the gain limb but is verified only on a secondary site. Nothing found permits killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge.

K3.label: Taught, provisionally and borderline (otherwise silent in counted texts)
K3.reason: Guru Nanak's Babarvani at ang 360 draws K3's line: fighting between the strong is not complained of, but slaughter of the defenceless is a wrong someone must answer for. It is Tier 1, and the text itself judges the slaughter wrong, so rule 4 does not reduce it to Implied. But it is a lament, not a rule, and it is VERIFIED (search) only through a SikhNet commentary, not on a Gurbani database. If a direct check fails, K3 is silent in counted texts. The Zafarnama (contested, not counted) speaks of the sword as a last resort, not of non-combatants. Fuller war ethics (sparing the fleeing, women and children; Bhai Ghanaiya's care for wounded enemies) are found in the Rahitnamas and Janamsakhi-type narratives, which corpus.md excludes. Those were not searched.

These are recorded as UNVERIFIED rows: ang 74 (Guru Arjan, 'Halemi Raj': no one shall attack or cause suffering to anyone), which would be the most direct counted text for K1 if confirmed; ang 1358 (anger as the root of strife); ang 386 (no ill will towards others); ang 145 (kings as butchers); ang 1105 (Kabir's warrior who fights for the dīn); ang 1350 (Kabir: why kill a chicken if God is in all); Bachitar Natak 6.43 (uprooting evil-doers). These should be checked first.
3. Gurmukhi given from memory. The Gurmukhi phrases for ang 1375, 1374, 1103, 1382, 1378, 140, 471, 360 and 787 were not displayed in the search results (only English renderings and ang numbers were). They should be checked against SearchGurbani or SikhiToTheMax before publication.
4. Weaker verifications. Ang 1375 is confirmed on sikhsamridhi.com and SikhiWiki, not yet on SearchGurbani or SikhiToTheMax. Ang 360 is confirmed only through a SikhNet commentary. Ang 199 is still verified only on Sikhri.org and was not re-checked. The ang for Kabir salok 187 differs by edition (1374 or 1375).
5. Not searched. The Ardas's 'sarbat da bhala' (Tier 2) was not checked in this pass. Nor were the Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, or the Dasam Granth beyond Zafarnama 22. Scripture verses in which God destroys slanderers or tyrants were not searched (for example the Sulhi Khan shabad, from memory ang 825, and the Prahlad and Harnakhas verses). These are divine acts, so rule 4 would make them context, but they should be listed for completeness. The 18th-century Rahitnamas (excluded) are said to contain harsher lines about Muslims; they were not checked and cannot decide anything, but the counter-evidence researcher may wish to note them.
6. Infanticide in scripture. No Guru Granth Sahib verse addressing infanticide directly was found. Tradition credits Guru Amar Das and later Gurus with opposing it, but that comes from non-counted sources. For newborns, K1 rests on the wider rules and on the Tier 2 Rehat Maryada.
7. Rehat Maryada details. Its article and item lettering differs between editions ((l) in two editions; reported as a different letter on the SGPC 'Gurmat Rehni' page). The Punjabi wording of the daughter clause was not seen. Whether non-SGPC groups (for example the Damdami Taksal, the Nihangs and the Namdharis) have equivalent clauses was not checked.
8. Strength rating. The direct Kabir texts on killing are aimed at ritual slaughter. A reviewer might rate them Implied for killing people rather than Clear teaching (wider rule). If so, K1 would rest on ang 1384 and 1427 alone. Those reach killing only by arguing from a lesser harm to a greater one, so the K1 result would become borderline.

rows.branch: all branches (every Sikh group accepts the Guru Granth Sahib)
rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1105, Rāg Mārū, salok of Bhagat Kabir that follows his shabads (salok number not confirmed)
rows.original: ਸੂਰਾ ਸੋ ਪਹਿਚਾਨੀਐ ਜੁ ਲਰੈ ਦੀਨ ਕੇ ਹੇਤ
rows.translation: Sant Singh Khalsa, as recorded in the project's earlier research; compared with a barusahib.org commentary
rows.says: The true hero is the one who fights for the sake of dīn and would rather be cut to pieces than leave the field. Sant Singh Khalsa gives dīn as "religion". Other Sikh readings give "the poor and helpless", and much Sikh exegesis also reads the battle as the inner fight against vice. The salok next to it describes the battle drum sounding in the sky of the mind.
rows.bearing: This is the Guru Granth Sahib's nearest approval of fighting. It is set on the battlefield, so it is context only (rule 5, war). It does not permit killing anyone who is not fighting. On the "helpless" reading it praises defending others, which K1's exception allows. The disputed word dīn (translations.md) does not change K1, because neither reading permits killing someone who is not attacking. It does not decide K1 or K0, and it says nothing about people who are not fighting (K3).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) in the project's earlier research (Article I) on SearchGurbani, ang 1105. In this session, searches confirmed that ang 1105 is Kabir's Rāg Mārū with the salok 'Gagan damāmā bājio', and found a barusahib.org commentary that places this line there. The line itself was not displayed in this session.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 825, Rāg Bilāval, Guru Arjan (Mahalla 5), shabad 'Sulhī te nārāiṇ rākh' (numbered ||2||18||104|| as reported)
rows.original: ਸੁਲਹੀ ਤੇ ਨਾਰਾਇਣ ਰਾਖੁ
rows.translation: Sant Singh Khalsa, as on SearchGurbani
rows.says: God saved the Guru from Sulhi, whom tradition identifies as Sulhi Khan, a Mughal officer. His plot failed and he died in disgrace. The Master drew his axe and cut off his head, and in an instant he was dust.
rows.bearing: The text approves this killing, but the killer is God, not a person acting on private authority. In the traditional reading the victim was moving against the Guru, so even as a model it falls within K1's defence exception. It gives no licence to any person and does not decide K1, K0 or K3 (rule 4). One modern Sikh scholar (Karminder Singh, Sikh Vichar Forum) argues that reading Sulhi as a person is a mistake. His reading is an individual's and carries no authority.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): SearchGurbani ang 825 (Raag Bilaval, Mahalla 5). The stanza about the axe was reported in the same search results.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, Rāg Bhairo, shabad on Prahlad (SearchGurbani shabad 4194, lines 6 to 7). Ang 1133 and authorship by Guru Amar Das are from memory and not confirmed. The line 'ਹਰਣਾਖਸੁ ਦੁਸਟੁ ਹਰਿ ਮਾਰਿਆ ਪ੍ਰਹਲਾਦੁ ਤਰਾਇਆ' is as given on SikhiWiki, with no ang shown.
rows.original: ਸਾਸਨਾ ਤੇ ਬਾਲਕੁ ਗਮੁ ਨ ਕਰੈ (SearchGurbani: saasanaa thae baalak gam n karai); ਹਰਣਾਖਸੁ ਦੁਸਟੁ ਹਰਿ ਮਾਰਿਆ
rows.translation: Sant Singh Khalsa, as on SearchGurbani; SikhiWiki for the second line
rows.says: Taught by the Guru, the child Prahlad keeps repeating God's name and does not fear punishment. In the story as the scripture tells it, his father, King Harnakhash (Hiranyakashipu), sets out to kill him for this, and God destroys the wicked father and saves the child.
rows.bearing: God kills a father who is attacking his own child, and the text approves it. But the act is God's, not a person's, and it rescues a child from a deadly attack, which is K1's own exception. If anything, the story presents a parent's attempt to kill a child as tyranny. That is Implied support for protecting children (rule 4) and is not counted. It does not decide any wording.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) for the Prahlad lines on SearchGurbani (shabad 4194, lines 6 to 7). The line on Harnakhash's killing was seen only on SikhiWiki, with no ang, so that part is UNVERIFIED. The detail that the father rushed at the child with a sword is from memory and UNVERIFIED.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, the Bābarvāṇī hymns of Guru Nanak: Rāg Āsā, ang 360; Rāg Āsā Aṣṭpadīāṅ, ang 417 to 418; Rāg Tilang, ang 722 ('ਪਾਪ ਕੀ ਜੰਞ ਲੈ ਕਾਬਲਹੁ ਧਾਇਆ', from memory)

rows.bearing: Context only (rule 5). These hymns condemn an army's slaughter and abuse of people who were not fighting. They are a lament, not a rule (rule 4), so at most they give Implied support for K3. They count towards no label.

rows.reference: Dasam Granth, Zafarnama (Guru Gobind Singh's Persian letter to Aurangzeb), couplet 22 in most editions (21 in some)
rows.original: chu kār az hama hīlate dar guzasht, halāl ast burdan ba shamshīr dast (Persian, as transliterated on SikhiWiki)
rows.translation: SikhiWiki, and two secondary articles (organiser.org; advocatetanmoy.com). The Kohli translation was not seen.
rows.says: When every other means has failed, it is lawful (or righteous) to take up the sword. The couplet explains why the Guru fought at Chamkaur. The letter also accuses the emperor's commanders of breaking oaths of safe conduct that they swore on the Qur'an.
rows.bearing: This is the tradition's classic statement that force is a last resort. It concerns war and armed resistance to an imperial army (rule 5, context only), and the text is not counted (rule 1). It does not permit killing anyone who is not fighting. Its complaint against broken oaths of safe conduct is Implied support for K3, since it condemns betraying people who were promised safety.

The "wicked" here are the opposing army at Bhangani, not people singled out for their faith or status. It does not decide K1 or K0, and it says nothing about people who are not fighting (K3).

Sikh readers take it together with the Guru's battles (rule 5, war) and as aimed at tyrants and oppressors, not at people for their faith. It gives no licence to private persons. rows.says: A prayer asking God to protect the devotee with his own hand and to destroy all the devotee's enemies. A further line, as recalled, asks God to strike down in battle all the evildoers who stir up strife, all the mlecchas. Mleccha is a word for barbarians or the impure, sometimes read as foreign invaders.

Mleccha is a disputed word: it can name a moral type or an ethnic or religious outsider. The text is Tier 2 and not counted (rule 1), and the mleccha line is unverified. It does not decide K1, K0 or K3, but it should be checked if the Dasam Granth's status is ever revisited.

rows.says: Keep away from the faithless person and run far from him. Elsewhere such a person is compared unfavourably with a pig.
rows.bearing: This is the Guru Granth Sahib's harshest language about a class of people, but it says to keep away, never to harm or kill. Sākat names a moral type, not a community (translations.md). It neither grades protection nor permits killing, so it does not decide any wording.

rows.translation: Official SGPC English translation, as quoted on secondary sites
rows.says: Anyone who keeps relations with groups hostile to the Panth (minas, masands, followers of Dhirmal or Ram Rai), with users of tobacco, or with killers of female infants is liable to chastisement and boycott. The same list includes anyone who gives a son or daughter in marriage for money.

The sanction is penance and social boycott through the community's discipline, not physical punishment, so the penalty side is court context (rule 5). The list also narrows fellowship with some groups, but it gives no licence to harm them (Article I, counter-evidence section K). Not counted.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1103, Rāg Mārū, Bhagat Kabir
rows.original: ਜੀਅ ਬਧਹੁ ਸੁ ਧਰਮੁ ਕਰਿ ਥਾਪਹੁ
rows.translation: Sant Singh Khalsa, as on SearchGurbani
rows.says: You kill living beings and call it righteous action. Then tell me, brother, what would you call unrighteous? The lines around it attack religious hypocrisy.
rows.bearing: This is the most direct counted text against killing found. It denies that killing living beings (jīa, which includes people) can be a religious duty, so it answers in advance any claim that religion licenses a killing. That makes it the tradition's own reply to rows 7 and 8. As a wider rule (rule 7) it reaches everyone. But its setting is probably ritual killing, and the tradition does not read it as forbidding all killing of animals, so its weight for K1 is borderline Clear teaching. For K0 it covers killing in the name of religion, but not killing for gain or out of anger.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): SearchGurbani ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir; the English rendering and the surrounding lines were shown

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid 129 to 130; and ang 1427, Salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur 16

rows.bearing: These are wider rules not to harm anyone, grounded in God's presence in all, so they reach every person (rule 7). They reach killing only as the gravest form of the harm they forbid. They are the tradition's own frame for reading every hard text above. For K1 they are Clear teaching (wider rule), but borderline; the support researcher should decide.

counter.reconciliation: No counted text was found that permits, commands or approves a deliberate killing that K1 forbids, so the tradition has no hard counted text here to limit or explain away. The Guru Granth Sahib (Tier 1, accepted by every Sikh group; the only counted text) approves killing in two places only. Both are God's acts against aggressors: Sulhi (ang 825), and the father Harnakhash, who was trying to kill his child Prahlad (Rāg Bhairo). Its one praise of fighting (Kabir, ang 1105) is set on the battlefield and qualified by "for the sake of dīn". Sant Singh Khalsa renders dīn as religion; other Sikh readers render it as the poor and helpless, and many also read the battle as the inner struggle (barusahib.org, a modern commentary with no authority). The Guru Granth Sahib's own frame for all of this is a set of wider rules owed to everyone: killing living beings cannot be called righteousness (Kabir, ang 1103); break no one's heart, because God dwells in all (Farid, ang 1384); frighten no one (Guru Tegh Bahadur, ang 1427); return good for evil and do not let anger settle (Farid, ang 1382); keep no ill will (Guru Arjan, ang 386); do not strike back (Farid, ang 1378). Its harshest words about a class of people, the faithless (sākat), tell the reader to keep away, never to harm, and the word names a moral type, not a community. The Dasam Granth (Tier 2, contested, not counted) is where the tradition's warrior teaching lives. The Zafarnama gives the classic rule that the sword is lawful only when every other means has failed, in a letter answering an imperial army that broke oaths of safe conduct. The Bachittar Natak and the Benti Chaupai speak of destroying the wicked and of God striking down enemies in battle. Sikh readers take all of these as war and the defence of the oppressed (rule 5), not as licence for private killing. One line of the Benti Chaupai, recalled as naming the mlecchas, could not be verified. The Vaaran Bhai Gurdas (Tier 2) record Guru Hargobind's turn to arms without speaking of killing. The Sikh Rehat Maryada (approved by the SGPC, the elected body that manages the gurdwaras, in 1945 and published in 1950) is the modern authoritative code for mainstream Khalsa Sikhs, but it is Tier 2 and not counted. It makes child protection explicit: a Sikh must not kill his daughter or keep relations with a killer of daughters, and such killers are put under the community's boycott. Its daily Ardas ends with a prayer for the good of all (sarbat da bhala). It permits no killing, and its disciplinary penalties are penance and boycott. corpus.md lists no authorised interpreting body for Sikhism, so no Akal Takht or SGPC ruling can narrow a counted text under decision 8, and none was checked. Commentators cited here are modern individuals or websites (barusahib.org; Karminder Singh on the Sulhi verse), and none carries the tradition's authority.

K1.label: Not contradicted; taught by a wider rule (rule 7), borderline
K1.reason: No counted text (the Guru Granth Sahib) was found that permits, commands or approves a killing by a private person of someone who is not attacking. Nor was any found that allows killing newborns or children, declares a killing blameless because of the victim's status, limits protection to Sikhs, or grades it by caste, sex or status. The only killings the Guru Granth Sahib approves are God's acts against aggressors (ang 825; the Prahlad story), which rule 4 and K1's own defence exception both cover. Its praise of the warrior (ang 1105) is battlefield context (rule 5). Support comes through wider rules that reach everyone: ang 1103 (killing living beings is not righteousness; verified), ang 1384 and ang 1427 (verified in earlier research), with the scope texts ang 1299 and ang 611. It is borderline because ang 1384 and ang 1427 reach killing only as the gravest form of the harm they forbid, and ang 1103 is probably aimed at ritual killing. If the support researcher judges that none of these teaches K1 at the level of Clear teaching, the label falls to "not contradicted, silent". No counted text names infanticide. The explicit ban on killing daughters is in the Rehat Maryada (Tier 2, not counted, rule 1). The hard texts of the Dasam Granth (Zafarnama 22; Bachittar Natak; Benti Chaupai) are war context and are not counted, so they cannot change this label.

K0.label: Not contradicted; taught (wider rule, rule 7)
K0.reason: Verified counted texts forbid acting from anger, ill will or revenge towards anyone, wrongdoers included: ang 1382 (return good for evil, do not let anger settle), ang 386 (keep no ill will towards another) and ang 1378 (do not strike back). Each is a wider rule that includes not killing out of anger, hatred or revenge. Ang 1103 adds that killing cannot be made righteous by religion. No counted text was found that approves killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. Killing "for your own gain" is covered only by the general wider rules (rows 13 and 14), not by a text that names gain.

K3.label: Not contradicted; silent
K3.reason: No counted text states a rule about sparing people who are not fighting, and none approves killing them. The Bābarvāṇī hymns (ang 360, 417 to 418 and 722) lament an invading army's slaughter and abuse of civilians, but they are laments (rule 4) and could not be verified in this session, so they are at most Implied support. Ang 1105 praises steadfastness in battle and says nothing about non-combatants. The Dasam Granth (not counted) gives the last-resort rule (Zafarnama 22) and condemns broken oaths of safe conduct (Implied support). Its prayers and battle narratives about destroying the wicked or the mlecchas are war texts, and the mleccha line is unverified; none of these was found to approve killing non-combatants.

counter.gaps: The session-wide search limit was reached after 18 searches; three further queries were refused and returned nothing. Leads left unchecked because of this: Qazi Nur Muhammad's Jangnama (1765), the hostile Muslim chronicler often cited as testifying that the Khalsa did not kill women, children or fleeing men (outside the corpus, historical context for K3); the Babarvani hymns at ang 360 and 722; Kabir's saloks against using force and calling it lawful (around ang 1374 to 1375) and against killing animals while saying God is in all (ang 1350); the Guru Granth Sahib's texts against caste pride (around ang 1127 to 1128); the Halemi Raj stanza (ang 74); the line in Bachittar Natak chapter 6 on uprooting the wicked; the Benti Chaupai line on the mlecchas; the Zafarnama couplets on the killing of the Guru's sons; the account of Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution (Bachittar Natak chapter 5), which is context for courts and rulers; and Bhai Gurdas's other vārs. Not searched at all: the 18th-century rahitnamas (excluded as evidence, but they may contain hard texts, for example about Muslims or about killers of daughters); the Charitropakhyan beyond the Benti Chaupai; any Akal Takht edict (hukamnama) or SGPC statement on killing, honour killing or female infanticide, including the Akal Takht's statements on female foeticide, which fall under exclusion (c) in any case; Sikh legal and disciplinary practice beyond the Rehat Maryada's penance and boycott. The Guru Granth Sahib was searched only through targeted queries, not read in full, so a hard passage could have been missed, though none is known to the researcher. Corpus question for the project lead: the Nihang orders and the Damdami Taksal are generally said to treat the whole Dasam Granth as Gurbani (general knowledge, not verified). If either were held to be a branch that treats it as primary (decisions 3 and 4), its war texts would become counted for that branch. On present evidence they are war context (rule 5) and would not change K1 or K0, but the unverified mleccha line in the Benti Chaupai should then be checked for K3. Several rows rest on verification from the project's earlier research (Article I and Q-002), not re-searched here, and three rows (Zafarnama, Benti Chaupai, Bhai Gurdas) are verified only on secondary sites (SikhiWiki, igurbani.com) and should be re-checked on SearchGurbani. The Prahlad row's killing line and the Sulhi row's axe stanza were seen only in search summaries.

verified.reconciliation:
Counted texts. The Guru Granth Sahib (Tier 1, accepted by every Sikh group) is the only counted text. No passage found in it permits, commands or approves a killing by a private person of someone who is not attacking. That holds for any class of victim: newborns, daughters, wives, servants, people of other faiths, the faithless (sākat) or 'the wicked'. The only killings it approves are God's acts against aggressors: Sulhi at ang 825, and Harnakhas in the Prahlad story. Both are unverified in this pass, and both fall under rule 4 and K1's own defence exception. Its one praise of fighting (Kabir, ang 1105) is set on the battlefield (rule 5).

Its teaching runs the other way, through wider rules owed to everyone. Break no heart and speak no harsh word, because the True Lord is in all (Farid, ang 1384). Killing living beings cannot be called righteousness (Kabir, ang 1103). Frighten no one (Guru Tegh Bahadur, ang 1427). Return good for evil and do not let anger settle (Farid, ang 1382). Do not strike back (Farid, ang 1378). The strong who bully the weak are condemned (Guru Arjan, ang 199). Scope is set as everyone: no one is an enemy or a stranger (ang 1299), and all are children of one Father (ang 611).

How the tradition reconciles non-violence with the sword. From Guru Hargobind onwards, armed force was accepted as a last resort against tyranny and in defence of the weak. The standard statement is Zafarnama 22, in the contested Dasam Granth, so it is context only and verified on secondary sites only: when every other means has failed, it is lawful to take the sword. This matches K1's exception plus exclusion (b). It does not license killing for gain, anger or revenge, which Farid rules out. The Dasam Granth's harder lines (uprooting the wicked, Bachittar Natak 6; destroying enemies and mlecchas, Benti Chaupai) are prayers to God or battle narratives. Sikh readers take them as war against tyranny. All are unverified in their specific wording and not counted.

How the tradition reads Kabir's verses on killing. Mainstream Khalsa Sikhs (SGPC) forbid only ritually slaughtered (kutha) meat. They read Kabir's verses on killing living beings (ang 1103, 1375) as a polemic against killing in the name of religion, not as a ban on all killing of animals. Guru Nanak's salok on quarrels over meat (ang 1289, unverified) is usually cited for this. Groups such as the Namdharis read the verses more widely (general knowledge, unverified). This narrowing concerns animals (exclusion (e)) and takes no person outside the verses. But it is why ang 1103 is rated only borderline as a wider rule for K1.

Households and newborns. The Sikh Rehat Maryada (SGPC, approved 1945, published 1950; Tier 2, not counted; a modern body's authority) explicitly forbids a Sikh to kill his daughter or keep relations with a killer of daughters, and puts such people under the community's chastisement. Its daily Ardas ends with a prayer for the good of all. Its penalties are penance and exclusion, not physical punishment. No Guru Granth Sahib verse naming infanticide was found, so for newborns K1 rests on the wider rules (rule 9). corpus.md lists no authorised interpreting body for Sikhism, so no Akal Takht or SGPC ruling can narrow a counted text under decision 8.

K1.label: Not contradicted; taught by a wider rule (rule 7), borderline
K1.reason: No counted text (Guru Granth Sahib) permits, commands or approves a private person's killing of anyone who is not attacking, or declares such a killing blameless because of the victim's faith, sex, age or status. The only approved killings are God's acts against aggressors (ang 825; the Prahlad story). Rule 4 and K1's exception cover them, and both are unverified in this pass. The label rests on two verified counted texts. (1) Ang 1384 (Farid: break no heart, because the True Lord is in all), a wider duty not to harm anyone. The project already counts it at Clear teaching (Article I row 11a) and as teaching 'do not injure' (households annex, L1). Killing is harm on every tradition's terms, so it reaches K1 and every person K1 protects, newborns included (rule 9). (2) Ang 1103 (Kabir: you kill living beings and call it righteousness, so what is unrighteous?). This is the only verified counted text that speaks directly of killing. It is borderline Clear teaching, because its setting is ritual killing. Ang 1427 (frighten no one) supports them. It is borderline for two reasons. Ang 1384 speaks of words and hearts and reaches killing as the gravest harm. Ang 1375 (Kabir on halāl killing) is now UNVERIFIED, and ang 74 (the 'Halemi Raj' ban on attacking anyone) remains UNVERIFIED. If a reviewer held that ang 1384 does not reach killing and that ang 1103 is confined to ritual sacrifice, the label would fall to 'not contradicted, silent'. That would not be 'unclear': no Sikh authority narrows these texts as regards killing people, so rule 6 does not apply. The narrowing reading concerns animals only (exclusion (e)). The Rehat Maryada's explicit ban on killing daughters is Tier 2 and is reported beside the label (rule 1). The Dasam Granth's war texts are context (rules 1 and 5).

K0.label: Not contradicted; taught (wider rule, rule 7)
K0.reason: Whatever teaches K1 also teaches K0, the narrower wording (ang 1384, 1103). In addition, verified counted texts address K0's motives directly as wider duties owed to everyone, wrongdoers included. Ang 1382 (Farid 78: answer evil with good; do not let anger fill your mind) covers the anger, hatred and revenge limbs. Ang 1378 (Farid: do not strike back at those who strike you) covers revenge. Ang 199 (Guru Arjan: the strong who bully the poor and weak are condemned; verified on a secondary site in the Q-002 check) supports the gain limb. Ang 386 (keep no ill will) is now UNVERIFIED (disputed in project records) but is not needed. No counted text was found that approves killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. This label is firmer than K1's, because the motive texts are direct.

K3.label: Not contradicted; silent
K3.reason: No verified counted text states a rule about sparing people who are not fighting, and none approves killing them. The Babarvani hymns (ang 360, 417 to 418, 722) lament an invading army's slaughter of the defenceless and draw K3's line ('if the strong strike the strong, no one grieves'). But the ang 360 line has not been seen on any Gurbani database, so it is UNVERIFIED. It is also a lament that frames the invasion as divine judgement, so at most it is borderline Implied (rule 4). If it is verified and rated Clear teaching, K3 would become 'taught, borderline'. Ang 1105 praises steadfastness in battle and says nothing about non-combatants. The Dasam Granth (not counted) gives the last-resort rule (Zafarnama 22) and condemns broken oaths of safe conduct, which is Implied support. Its battle narratives and prayers about destroying the wicked or the mlecchas are unverified in wording, and none was found to approve killing non-combatants.

verified.branch_notes: Every Sikh group accepts the Guru Granth Sahib, so every counted row applies to all branches, and the labels are the same for all of them. Branch-specific material is all Tier 2 or outside the corpus. (1) Mainstream Khalsa Sikhs (SGPC, Akal Takht) follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada: the ban on killing daughters, the kutha rule and the Ardas. These are reported, not counted. (2) Namdharis are said to read Kabir's verses on killing living beings as a ban on all killing for food (general knowledge, unverified). That is a stricter reading and would only strengthen K1 for them. (3) The Nihang orders and the Damdami Taksal are said to treat the whole Dasam Granth as Gurbani (general knowledge, unverified), and the Nihangs also the Sarbloh Granth. If either counts as a branch under decision 3 that treats these texts as primary under decision 4, the Bachittar Natak and Benti Chaupai war texts would count for that branch. On present evidence they are prayers to God or battle narratives (rules 4 and 5), so K1 and K0 would not change. The unverified mleccha line in the Benti Chaupai should then be checked for K3. Not checked: the Namdhari, Nihang, Damdami Taksal, Udasi and Nirmala codes of conduct, and whether any has an equivalent of the kuṛī-mār clause.
verified.fairness_notes:
1. Verification asymmetry. This verifier could make no searches (the session-wide limit had been reached). Rows seen by only one researcher in this round were therefore marked UNVERIFIED, among them ang 1375, which the support researcher had found. That reflects a tooling limit, not evidence against the rows. If other traditions' verifiers could search, Sikhism should be re-checked before results are compared, so that it is not judged on fewer confirmed texts by accident.
2. Consistency with Article I and the households annex. The project already counts ang 1384 as a wider duty not to harm (Article I row 11a; annex L1, 'do not injure'). Refusing it for killing would treat the same verse differently from one article to the next. The annex refused only the step from harsh words to moderate blows (L3), for a reason special to L3. If the project decides that ang 1384 does not reach killing, it should apply the same test to other traditions' 'harm no one' sayings.
3. Polemics against ritual killing. Kabir's verses (ang 1103, 1375) are polemics against killing in the name of religion. An adherent could object if they were discounted while other traditions' general precepts against killing living beings are counted at full strength. Equally, a sceptic could object if a polemic were treated as a general precept. The fair test, applied to all traditions, is whether the text states its premise ('killing living beings is not righteousness') generally. Here it does, but in a ritual setting, so it is rated borderline.
4. Divine acts. Verses in which God kills Sulhi, Harnakhas, slanderers or the wicked must not be presented as approval of human killing. This matches rule 4 and how other traditions' divine-judgement texts are handled.
5. Disputed words. Rendering mleccha as 'Muslims', dusht as a religious group or sākat as a sect would make texts look like faith-based targeting. Each is disputed, and translations.md flags sākat and dīn.
6. Tier 2 weight. The Rehat Maryada states the clearest Sikh rule on household killing (no killing of daughters), but it is Tier 2 and not counted. That is consistent with other traditions' Tier 2 codes, but an adherent may feel the tradition's official code is undervalued. Article II should say plainly that it supports the counted result.
7. Teaching style. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches through devotional poetry, not legal rules, so its absence of a worded rule against murder should not be read as silence. The Clear teaching category exists for this, and it should not be stretched either.
